research_text:
## Research brief

### API and reported value

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation and creates socket factories or `SSLEngine` instances. Its `init(KeyManager[], TrustManager[], SecureRandom)` method receives key managers, **peer-authentication trust managers**, and a randomness source. The reported finding concerns the second argument—the `TrustManager[]` supplied at initialization—not a negotiated protocol or handshake result. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The supplied detector message says an application-defined manager was present and was not observed coming from a factory. The CrySL file itself does **not** contain that class-origin test or the diagnostic label `UnsatisfiedConstraint`; it requires the predicate `generatedTrustManagers[tm]`. The file alone does not establish how a particular detector derived or presented the finding. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

### Documented usage and remediation guidance

Oracle documents both factory-created and application-implemented trust managers as valid API usage. A custom `X509TrustManager` must make the documented certificate-path trust decisions; being application-defined is not, by itself, an API violation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?source=%3Aow%3Alp%3Acpo%3A%3A&utm_source=openai))

Documented alternatives include:

- Initialize a `TrustManagerFactory` with appropriate trust material and pass its `getTrustManagers()` result to the context. Oracle documents PKIX factory managers for certificate-path validation.
- Pass `null` for `tm` to `SSLContext.init`; the API documents provider-selected default trust-manager-factory behavior. Oracle’s SunJSSE documentation describes how default trust material is located. This can change which peers are trusted, so it is not necessarily equivalent to a custom manager.
- Where custom behavior is required, Oracle also documents implementations that delegate to a factory-generated manager. The documentation does not prescribe one universal replacement for every custom implementation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?source=%3Aow%3Alp%3Acpo%3A%3A&utm_source=openai))

Certificate-chain trust and endpoint identity are distinct. Oracle says raw `SSLSocket` and `SSLEngine` use must also check the peer’s identity; HTTPS endpoint identification is available during the handshake. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))

Sources: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html` and `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html`.

### Exact CrySL rule

The supplied primary rule is at `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl`.

Its relevant matching and requirement clauses are, verbatim: ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

```text
SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext
```

```text
	i1: init(km, tm, random);
	Init := i1;
```

```text
REQUIRES
	generatedKeyManagers[km];
	generatedTrustManagers[tm];
	randomized[random];
```

The file declares `km`, `tm`, and `random` as `KeyManager[]`, `TrustManager[]`, and `SecureRandom`, respectively. Thus the `Init` event is **parameter-constrained**, not an unconstrained match on the name `init`. The rule is scoped to `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`: **it does not specify a match for an unrelated method merely because it shares that name**. The file itself does not explain detector-specific method resolution or subtype handling. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The other declared events are static `getInstance` with one argument or two arguments, and `createSSLEngine` with zero or two arguments; the underscores leave the corresponding values unspecified in the rule. The file forbids `getDefault()`, orders the events as `Get, Init, Engine?`, and constrains `protocol` to the literal strings `"TLSv1.2"` or `"TLSv1.3"`. It also declares the three quoted requirements and two resulting predicates. It does not define `generatedTrustManagers` in this file or state that a custom manager is categorically invalid. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The protocol constraint is a test of the **requested string**, not a statement of enabled or negotiated versions. Oracle documents that even a version-named context may support other versions. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))

### Compatibility and migration

- **Trust material and persisted formats:** Changing the selected trust manager can change trust decisions. The cited `SSLContext` documentation does not specify a required persisted-format conversion for that change. Separately, Oracle documents PKCS12 as the JDK’s recommended keystore format and `keytool -importkeystore` as a migration mechanism; that is not presented as a prerequisite for changing an `SSLContext` trust manager. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?source=:ow:lp:cpo::))
- **Wire compatibility:** Oracle documents TLS 1.3 compatibility differences from earlier versions, including close behavior, certificate-signature support, and cipher suites. These are relevant if the enabled or negotiated protocol changes; the trust-manager finding alone does not establish such a change. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?source=:ow:lp:cpo::))
- **Platform support:** `SSLContext` is documented since Java 1.4. Oracle documents TLS 1.3 in JDK 11 and in JDK 8u261 and later; support and enabled defaults must be checked for the actual runtime and provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Compatibility sources: `https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/security/java-cryptography-architecture-jca-reference-guide.html` and `https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/11-relnote-issues.html`.

**Unresolved:** The linked rule is on a moving `master` branch. Its retrieved contents were not independently hash-verified against the supplied SHA-256, and the compiled rule artifact, detector version, and raw diagnostic were not supplied. The rule source therefore cannot independently verify the reported detector message or its provenance analysis.
